summary:
What happens to a spacecraft’s story when its mission ends? Developed by Become-TECH, Son Sinyal (The Last Signal) is a browser-based 3D educational game that helps children aged 7–15 discover the stories of NASA equipment left on the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

Set in a fictional 2060 resource crisis, the game follows astronaut Becker as players explore historical missions, listen to equipment tell its story, and solve short puzzles about its purpose and scientific contributions. Players then bring educational samples to Earth and complete a simplified recycling activity.

NASA mission records, technical documents, and 3D resources inform the game’s scientific content. Historical facts are distinguished from fictional dialogue, recovery journeys, and recycling scenarios. An in-game archive connects discoveries to their NASA sources.

Addressing “Abandoned but Not Forgotten,” our project turns scattered technical information into an interactive learning experience. Its central message is that a mission may end, but the knowledge it leaves behind still matters.
details:
THE PROBLEM AND OUR APPROACH

NASA’s past missions have left equipment on the Moon, Mars, and elsewhere in space. These objects represent scientific achievements, engineering decisions, and stories of exploration. However, young learners may find those stories difficult to discover when information is spread across technical documents and separate mission archives.

Become-TECH developed Son Sinyal (The Last Signal) to make these stories accessible through exploration, storytelling, and simple puzzles. Our primary audience is children aged 7–15.

HOW THE GAME WORKS

The game takes place in a fictional 2060, when Earth faces a severe shortage of raw materials. Players control astronaut Becker, beginning at an Earth station and following a chronological sequence of historical missions across lunar, Martian, and space environments.

When players approach equipment, they scan it and hear a short first-person story accompanied by on-screen text. They then solve brief puzzles about the equipment’s function or scientific contribution. These activities ask players to use the information they have just encountered.

The prototype includes 14 historical mission encounters, with examples such as Surveyor 3, Apollo equipment, Viking 1, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, and Ingenuity. Players transport mission-related educational loads back to Earth and complete a simplified cleaning, sorting, and recycling activity. A further scenario introduces Dacron mesh documented among Perseverance’s landing debris.

An in-game mission archive lets players revisit completed stories, equipment information, scientific results, and NASA source links.

HOW WE USE NASA RESOURCES

Our scientific content draws on NASA mission pages, NASA/JPL resources, NSSDCA records, technical publications, and NASA 3D resources. These sources inform mission histories, equipment functions, location references, and material descriptions.

We distinguish historical information from the game’s creative interpretation. The 2060 crisis, equipment dialogue, recovery journeys, and simplified recycling activities are fictional educational scenarios. Terrain and travel distances are adapted for gameplay. The game does not present its activities as NASA-approved procedures for collecting or recycling historical spacecraft.

CREATIVITY AND INTENDED IMPACT

Our central creative choice is to let equipment introduce its own history. Instead of encountering an unexplained object, players meet a narrator with a purpose, a scientific contribution, and a story worth remembering.

The recycling storyline connects past exploration with questions about future resource use. It supports the “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” theme by encouraging players to value both the equipment and the knowledge it represents.

Our intended impact is to encourage curiosity about space exploration and help young learners connect scientific information with meaningful decisions. We have not yet measured learning gains; a future evaluation could compare understanding before and after play.

TOOLS AND DEVELOPMENT

Son Sinyal uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js and WebGL for its 3D environments. Player progress is stored locally in the browser. Blender and Python supported the preparation of fictional models and asset conversion. The recycling facility also uses assets from Kenney’s CC0 Factory Kit.

ChatGPT/Codex and Claude assisted with research organization, coding, debugging, interface design, and asset preparation. The team directed the concept, audience, narrative, and design revisions. The current game uses prepared dialogue and rule-based interactions rather than a live conversational AI model.

DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

We prioritized short explanations, readable text, large interaction buttons, subtitles, and opportunities to retry after an incorrect answer. Complex calculations were replaced with simpler questions about equipment functions. A selectable voice-guidance mode supports the opening mission, although comprehensive accessibility testing remains future work.

The project aims to make one idea memorable: the end of a mission does not mean the end of its story.
